0.0.n: A friendly way to address a young adult man here, rather than referring to an older brother.

0.2.n: 枚 counts flat objects, including tickets; the object being counted is understood here.

0.3.n: The conditional form of ある describes having a ticket as the condition for being okay.

0.4.n: Usually expresses being okay; here it reassures the listener that no additional ticket is needed.

0.5.n: Adds politeness to the reassurance 大丈夫.

1.0.n: Signals a reaction to newly heard information.

1.2.n: Refers back to what the other person just said.

1.3.n: Part of そうなんですか; な links そう to explanatory ん, expressing interest in newly learned information.

1.4.n: A casual shortening of ですか used here to ask for confirmation.

1.6.n: 枚 is the counter used for flat items such as tickets.

1.7.n: Marks one ticket as the amount being checked for sufficiency.

1.8.n: In でいい, it asks whether the stated amount is sufficient or acceptable.

1.9.n: Casually shortens ですか, giving the question a relaxed but somewhat polite tone.

2.0.n: A common conversational version of すみません, used here to politely get attention.

3.0.n: 階 counts floors in a building.

3.1.n: Marks the location where the activity can take place.

3.2.n: Describes 手裏剣 as an activity available on the second floor.

3.3.n: Literally a throwing star; here the object stands for the activity of throwing it.

3.4.n: Links the shuriken activity to the ticket that permits it.

3.5.n: A borrowed word written in katakana, referring to admission to the activity.

3.6.n: Politely identifies what the ticket is for.

4.0.n: Repeats the location from the previous explanation, with questioning intonation.

4.1.n: Marks where the activity would happen, just as in the previous line.

4.2.n: The speaker starts repeating できる but trails off before finishing the word.

5.0.n: A very casual, typically masculine way to refer to yourself.

5.1.n: 第 turns the number into an ordered position, labeling which stage this is.

5.2.n: A katakana word for a game level or phase; the destination particle に is omitted after it here.

5.3.n: Past form of 進む; む changes to んだ in this form.

5.4.n: Short for explanatory の, presenting the completed advance as something the speaker is explaining or realizing.

5.5.n: Completes explanatory んだ in a plain, casual style.

5.7.n: Placed at the end as an afterthought specifying when the advance happened.

0.lit: Sir, if you have one ticket, it is okay.
0.tip: あったら sets a condition: having one ticket is enough.

1.lit: Oh, is that so? With one ticket, is it fine?
1.tip: すか is a casual shortening of ですか that you will hear in relaxed speech.

2.tip: すいません is a common spoken version of the standard すみません.

3.lit: It is a ticket for shuriken you can do on the second floor.
3.tip: The description 2階でできる comes before 手裏剣, telling you where that activity is available.

4.lit: On the second floor, can do…?
4.tip: The unfinished でき echoes できる from the previous line as the speaker checks what they heard.

5.lit: I advanced to the second stage, you see, just now.
5.tip: 進んだんだ combines past 進んだ with explanatory んだ; the repeated sounds serve different purposes.
